specAnchors.text: be able to classify reactions (including those in Unit 1) as addition, elimination, substitution, oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis or polymerisation

primer.text: Organic reactions sort into families by their bookkeeping: addition merges, elimination splits, substitution swaps, redox climbs and falls, hydrolysis lets water wedge, polymerisation chains. This note runs each family through its signature equation so classification becomes instant.

modules.title: Addition and elimination: molecular bookkeeping
modules.opening: Two reactants collapsing into one product is the addition signature; one reactant sprouting extra products - typically an alkene plus a small castoff - is elimination. Ethene's conversions give both patterns their textbook examples.
keyPoints: Addition reactions combine two reactants into a single product, classically across the alkene double bond.
Ethene adds hydrogen to give ethane, bromine to give 1,2-dibromoethane, and water to give ethanol.
Elimination reactions produce more products than reactants, usually an alkene plus a small molecule.
Bromoethane with hydroxide under ethanolic conditions eliminates to ethene, water and bromide.

low.restatement: Addition merges everything into one molecule (nothing discarded); elimination throws a small molecule out and leaves a double bond behind.
low.analogy: Addition snaps two LEGO bricks into one assembly; elimination pries one brick off an assembly, leaving a hole (the double bond) behind.
low.examPointer: Count reactant and product species when classifying: 2-to-1 signals addition, 1-to-2+ signals elimination.

medium.restatement: Addition saturates the double bond by spreading two new substituents across it; elimination desaturates by carving a new double bond from adjacent carbons while ejecting a small molecule such as water or a hydrogen halide.
medium.analogy: Addition zips a jacket shut across an open gap; elimination unzips a new gap where none existed.
medium.examPointer: Spot the double bond: formed in elimination, consumed in addition - that is the structural tell for classification questions.

modules.title: Substitution and oxidation: swaps and electron loss
modules.opening: Substitution swaps one atom or group for another; oxidation hands the organic molecule to an oxidising agent, tracked as oxygen gain or hydrogen loss. Bromoethane to ethanol shows the swap; ethanal to ethanoic acid shows the climb.
keyPoints: Substitution swaps an atom or group inside the compound for a different atom or group.
CH3CH2Br + OH- -> C2H5OH + Br- swaps bromide for hydroxide.
Organic oxidation can involve loss of hydrogen or gain of oxygen, driven by an oxidising agent such as acidified dichromate, Fehling's or Tollens'.
CH3CHO + [O] -> CH3COOH oxidises the aldehyde to the acid.

low.restatement: A substitution is an exchange at one position on the carbon skeleton; oxidation raises the oxygen content or lowers the hydrogen content of the whole molecule.
low.analogy: Substitution is swapping a house's front door; oxidation is renovating the house by adding a floor (oxygen) or removing bricks (hydrogen).
low.examPointer: The [O] notation stands for the oxidising agent's oxygen equivalent - name a real reagent (acidified dichromate(VI), Fehling's, Tollens') when asked.

medium.restatement: Substitution conserves the carbon skeleton while trading functional groups; oxidation moves the molecule up the oxidation ladder (alkane -> alcohol -> aldehyde -> acid). The oxidising agent is reduced in the same transaction.
medium.analogy: A tenant swap in one room versus a whole-building renovation: substitution trades one fixture, oxidation transforms the building's energy rating.
medium.examPointer: Quote the C2H4Br2-free example equation CH3CHO + [O] -> CH3COOH and name at least one oxidising agent.

modules.title: Reduction and hydrolysis: hydrogen gain and water splitting
modules.opening: Reduction is oxidation's mirror: hydrogen gained or oxygen lost, often with lithium aluminium hydride supplying the [H]. Hydrolysis sounds like water doing the splitting - and with chloromethane it does, yielding methanol and hydrogen chloride.
keyPoints: Organic reduction can involve gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen.
CH3CHO + [H] -> CH3CH2OH reduces the aldehyde to the primary alcohol, the [H] often from lithium aluminium hydride.
Hydrolysis is a reaction with water that splits a compound, e.g. CH3Cl + H2O -> CH3OH + HCl.
The name hydrolysis means splitting (lysis) by water (hydro).

low.restatement: Reduction descends the oxidation ladder - aldehyde back to alcohol - via hydrogen gain or oxygen loss; hydrolysis invites water to cleave a bond and deliver its halves to the fragments.
low.analogy: Reduction is undressing the molecule of oxygen or dressing it in hydrogen; hydrolysis is letting water act as the splitting wedge.
low.examPointer: Keep the [H] agent straight: lithium aluminium hydride reduces; dichromate oxidises - reversing them is a classic error.

medium.restatement: Hydrogen addition saturates or deoxygenates the substrate; water's split into H and OH fragments installs them across the broken bond, as chloromethane shows with methanol and HCl as products.
medium.analogy: Water arrives as a two-handed helper, giving one hand (OH) to the carbon and the other (H) to the departing group.
medium.examPointer: Quote the chloromethane example when defining hydrolysis - it is the note's canonical case.

modules.title: Addition polymerisation: monomers into chains
modules.opening: Addition polymerisation is addition iterated: alkene double bonds break open and chain together into poly(alkenes), the plastic family. One monomer's repeat unit echoes down a chain thousands long.
keyPoints: At AS level, addition polymerisation is the known polymerisation type.
Each monomer spends its alkene double bond, opening it to link into the growing chain.
The repeat unit mirrors the monomer minus its double bond, repeated along the chain.
Poly(alkenes) such as poly(1,2-dichloroethene) form from the corresponding substituted alkenes.

low.restatement: Every monomer donates its double bond to the chain; the polymer's backbone is single bonds with each repeat unit carrying the monomer's substituents.
low.analogy: Paperclips with a hook (double bond) that interlocks into a long strip: each clip spends its hook joining to neighbours.
low.examPointer: When drawing polymers, strip the C=C from the repeat unit and add continuing bonds through the brackets.

medium.restatement: Polymerisation conserves atoms exactly - the chain is the monomer collection linked end to end. Substituents (chlorine atoms in dichloroethene) ride along unchanged on the saturated backbone.
medium.analogy: A train built from identical carriages: each carriage (repeat unit) keeps its passengers (substituents) while couplings (single bonds) replace the open hooks (double bonds).
medium.examPointer: Check atom conservation in repeat-unit questions: nothing is lost in addition polymerisation.

glossary.definition: A reaction joining two reactants into a single product, typically across the alkene double bond.
A reaction removing a small molecule from a larger one, leaving an alkene and the castoff fragment.
A reaction in which water splits a compound into fragments.
Chain growth where alkene monomers open their double bonds and link end to end into a saturated backbone.
